She has been suffering ___ dengue for the past week.
The verb 'suffer' takes the preposition 'from' before the name of an illness.
The ship is bound ___ Mumbai and will dock there tomorrow.
'Bound for' is a fixed expression meaning travelling towards a destination.
The scheme was launched ___ the aegis of the Ministry of Finance.
'Under the aegis of' is a fixed prepositional phrase meaning under the protection or sponsorship of.
The committee consists ___ ten members, including two external experts.
'Consist of' is used when listing the parts that make up a whole.
She is not eligible ___ the post of manager because she lacks the required experience.
The adjective 'eligible' is followed by 'for' before a post or benefit.
The manager was angry ___ the clerk for the delay in processing the file.
We are 'angry with' a person and 'angry at/about' a thing or situation.
She is capable ___ handling the entire assignment on her own.
'Capable' is followed by 'of' and a gerund, not by an infinitive.
She insisted ___ paying the bill herself despite our protests.
The verb 'insist' takes the preposition 'on' before a noun or gerund.
The teacher was displeased ___ the student's careless conduct.
'Displeased with' is used before a person or behaviour that causes dissatisfaction.
He was accused ___ stealing money from the office locker.
The verb 'accuse' is followed by 'of' and the act or crime.
The novel was written ___ Ruskin Bond in the 1950s.
In the passive voice, the agent of an action is introduced by 'by'.
She is very fond ___ classical music and attends concerts regularly.
The adjective 'fond' is always followed by 'of'.
The prisoner was deprived ___ his liberty without any trial.
'Deprive of' is the correct collocation meaning to take something away from someone.
She is married ___ an engineer who works in a private firm.
In standard English, one is 'married to' another person.
The police are looking ___ the missing child in the nearby forest.
'Look for' means to search for someone or something.
He is good ___ solving difficult puzzles within seconds.
'Good at' is used before a skill or activity.
She has been living in Delhi ___ 2018 and knows the city well.
'Since' is used with a point of time in the past, whereas 'for' is used with a duration.
The meeting will be over ___ 5 p.m., so please come before that.
'By' means not later than a particular time.
He has been waiting ___ the bus for half an hour.
'Wait for' is the correct prepositional verb meaning to await someone or something.
The sweets were distributed ___ the four children equally.
'Among' is used when more than two persons or things are involved.
The property was divided ___ the two brothers after their father's death.
'Between' is used for two persons or things, while 'among' is used for more than two.
She sat ___ me during the entire lecture and took detailed notes.
'Beside' means next to, whereas 'besides' means in addition to.
___ English, she also knows French and German.
'Besides' means in addition to, which fits the meaning of the sentence.
Identify the preposition in the sentence: The cat slept under the wooden table.
'Under' shows the relation of place between the cat and the table, so it is a preposition.
Which of the following is a preposition of time?
'At' can indicate time (at 5 p.m.), while the other options indicate place or direction.
Choose the sentence that correctly uses a preposition after the adjective good.
A) She is good in mathematics.
B) She is good at mathematics.
C) She is good on mathematics.
D) She is good for mathematics.
E) She is good with mathematics.
The correct collocation is 'good at' a subject or skill.
Choose the sentence that correctly uses a preposition after the adjective afraid.
A) He is afraid from darkness.
B) He is afraid with darkness.
C) He is afraid of darkness.
D) He is afraid at darkness.
E) He is afraid to darkness.
Choose the sentence that correctly uses a preposition after the verb insist.
A) She insisted to pay the bill.
B) She insisted for paying the bill.
C) She insisted at paying the bill.
D) She insisted on paying the bill.
E) She insisted in paying the bill.
'Insist on' is followed by a gerund, so 'insisted on paying' is correct.
The teacher was angry (A)/ on the students (B)/ because they had not (C)/ completed the assignment. (D)/ No error (E)
Replace 'on' with 'with': one is angry with a person.
She has been (A)/ working in this office (B)/ since five years (C)/ without any leave. (D)/ No error (E)
Use 'for' with a duration: 'for five years'. 'Since' requires a point of time.
The two sisters (A)/ divided the property (B)/ among themselves (C)/ without any dispute. (D)/ No error (E)
For exactly two people, 'between' is used: 'between themselves'.
He is capable (A)/ to solve (B)/ the problem (C)/ on his own. (D)/ No error (E)
'Capable' takes 'of + gerund', so it should be 'of solving'.
The students were (A)/ discussing about (B)/ the new syllabus (C)/ in the classroom. (D)/ No error (E)
'Discuss' is a transitive verb and does not take the preposition 'about'.
The Dead Sea lies ___ sea level, which makes it the lowest point on land.
'Below sea level' is the standard expression for a level lower than the sea.
The train passed ___ a long tunnel before reaching the station.
'Through' indicates movement inside and along the length of something.
She apologised ___ her rude behaviour at the meeting.
One apologises 'for' an action or fault and 'to' the person affected.
The accountant is responsible ___ preparing the annual financial report.
'Responsible for' is used before a task or duty.
The principal congratulated the students ___ their outstanding success.
'Congratulate someone on something' is the correct collocation.
The committee acted ___ accordance with the rules laid down by the board.
The fixed phrase is 'in accordance with'.
'In lieu of' means in place of or instead of something.
